newsitem.title: UK: BP sees bright future in Colombia despite strikes.
newsitem.headline: BP sees bright future in Colombia despite strikes.

text.p: British Petroleum, the single largest foreign investor in Colombia, said on Tuesday it saw a bright future for its operations in the troubled South American country despite continuing political uncertainty.

"In my experience, Colombia has to be one of the most complicated places to operate in the world... As a piece of business it is beneficial to BP, not just today but tomorrow, and also beneficial to Colombia," BP's chief executive John Browne told reporters after presenting 1996 financial results.

He spoke before Colombian guerillas, who have in the past attacked the country's oil interests, pledged to back a public sector strike. Colombia's second largest guerrilla force, the National Liberation Army (ELN) threatened "violence and grassroots disobedience."

The ELN, which was formed in the mid 1960s and specialises in sabotaging oil infrastructure and attacks on multinational enterprises, said its declaration of support was a precursor to what it termed a "national armed strike."
BP said oil production at its Cusiana and Cupiagua fields in Colombia's eastern plains region, running at about 170,000 barrels per day (bpd), was unaffected by the strike.
Exports via a pipeline operated by state-run oil company Ecopetrol to the Caribbean terminal of Covenas were also normal, BP said.
The British oil giant has pledged to invest $600 million in phase two development of Cusiana-Cupiagua in 1997, and confirmed on Tuesday that it was on track to more than double output.
"Production is currently on schedule to build up to 500,000 bpd by the end of the year," said Dick Olver, deputy chief executive of BP Exploration.

"It is clear that this is a wonderful project for the people of Colombia if it can be brought into operation continuously -- 85 percent of the value will go to the Colombian people one way or the other," said BP chairman David Simon.
Browne said the success of BP's Colombia operations depended to a large extent on winning the trust of local people.
He said BP was planning to invest $20 million in social projects this year in Colombia, "on top of the $100 million the local community will be getting from royalties."
Last month, Colombia's chief prosecutor launched an investigation into allegations that BP had funded paramilitary groups, claims described by BP as "injurious and offensive."
Simon said the company's most important short-term concern was to ensure the safety of its employees.
"We have done what is necessary for the security of BP staff. We have clear rules as to what we believe is ethical behaviour," he said.

"The board has absolute confidence in the staff and how they approach these problems. It then becomes a question about the (Colombian) government's capacity to perform in an appropriate and resolute manner on the problems they have to face."
